stem: A previously normotensive pregnant client at 32 weeks has repeated blood pressures of 148/94 mm Hg, new proteinuria, a severe headache that persists despite medication, and visual spots. Which classification is most accurate?

options.A: Preeclampsia with severe features because the persistent medication-unresponsive headache and visual symptoms are severe features.
options.B: Preeclampsia without severe features because the blood pressure is below 160/110 mm Hg.
options.C: Gestational hypertension because severe-range blood pressure is required before preeclampsia can be diagnosed.
options.D: Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia because hypertension first appeared during this pregnancy.

rationale: ACOG defines gestational hypertension as new hypertension after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive patient, and preeclampsia as hypertension with proteinuria or other evidence of organ involvement. ACOG identifies a new-onset severe headache unresponsive to medication and visual disturbances as severe features of preeclampsia. Severe-range blood pressure is one possible severe feature but is not required when another severe feature is present. Chronic hypertension, by contrast, is present before pregnancy or develops before 20 weeks, so a first presentation at 32 weeks in a previously normotensive client does not fit chronic hypertension.
educational_objective: Classify preeclampsia with severe features when new hypertension after 20 weeks is accompanied by proteinuria and severe neurologic features, even if blood pressure is below the severe-range threshold.
source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
source_document_title: Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy; Hypertensive Disorders — Criteria for Preeclampsia With Severe Features
source_locator: FAQ → Gestational Hypertension; 'What are the signs and symptoms of preeclampsia?' severe-features list; ACOG District IV Hypertensive Disorders → Criteria for Preeclampsia +/- Severe Features and Box 3.
source_claim_supported: ACOG identifies hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria/end-organ findings as preeclampsia and lists medication-unresponsive new headache and visual disturbances as severe features; severe-range BP is an alternative severe feature rather than a prerequisite when other severe features are present.

source_original.stem: A previously normotensive pregnant client at 32 weeks has repeated blood pressures of 148/94 mm Hg, new proteinuria, a severe headache that persists despite medication, and visual spots. Which classification is most accurate?

options.A: Preeclampsia with severe features because persistent severe headache and visual symptoms qualify as severe features.
options.B: Preeclampsia without severe features because the blood pressure has not reached the severe range of 160/110 mm Hg.
options.C: Gestational hypertension with severe features because proteinuria does not change the hypertensive diagnosis.
options.D: Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia because hypertension first appeared during this pregnancy.

source_original.rationale: ACOG describes preeclampsia as hypertension arising after 20 weeks with findings such as proteinuria and identifies severe headache and visual changes as severe features. Option A is therefore the best classification even though the blood pressure itself is below the severe-range threshold. Option B incorrectly ignores severe neurologic features. Option C is inferior because proteinuria supports preeclampsia rather than isolated gestational hypertension. Option D is incorrect because chronic hypertension is present before pregnancy or develops before 20 weeks, not first recognized at 32 weeks in a previously normotensive client.
source_original.source_detail: ACOG Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy — hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria/organ findings; severe features include persistent severe headache and visual symptoms. correction_summary: Retained the stem and key. Replaced the nonstandard distractor phrase 'gestational hypertension with severe features' with a cleaner diagnostic error and explicitly tied the severe-feature classification to medication-unresponsive headache and visual disturbance. Preserved the exact 160/110 mm Hg threshold only where ACOG directly supports it.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — preeclampsia with severe features
audit_findings.currentness: ACOG pages were live and rechecked 2026-08-16; no newer conflicting ACOG criteria identified.
audit_findings.exact_locator: ACOG severe-features list and formal criteria page directly support headache, visual symptoms, proteinuria, and BP thresholds.
audit_findings.claim_audit: All numeric BP thresholds and timing claims are directly sourced; no proteinuria quantity or lab threshold was introduced.

distractor_audit.A: Uniquely matches preeclampsia plus severe neurologic features.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because severe features can be present without severe-range BP.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because preeclampsia can be diagnosed without severe-range BP when hypertension plus proteinuria is present.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because hypertension first appearing at 32 weeks in a previously normotensive client is not chronic hypertension.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A accounts for both preeclampsia and the severe neurologic findings.
audit_findings.cueing: All four options are competing hypertensive classifications.
audit_findings.blueprint: Direct Physiological Adaptation relevance through an acute pregnancy complication.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial reread verified the severe-feature criteria and ensured the item does not imply 160/110 is necessary for severe-feature classification.
